variants.title: Look up the owner
variants.context: Consistent hashing hashes keys and node tokens into one ordered space. A key belongs to the first token at or after its position, wrapping around at the end. Every participant must use the same hash and token map.
variants.prompt: A cache key arrives. Put the lookup in order.

items.text: Take the stable key that must keep the same owner.
Hash it and map the result into the ring’s numeric range.
Find the first token at or after that position, wrapping past the end.
Send the request to the node behind that token.

variants.hint: The key is fixed first, then hashed, then matched to a token.
variants.explanation: Stable key → hash position → first token clockwise → physical owner. Every router must follow the same steps with the same token map to agree on ownership.

variants.title: Look up the owner
variants.context: Consistent hashing hashes keys and node tokens into one ordered space. A key belongs to the first token at or after its position, wrapping around at the end. Every participant must use the same hash and token map.
variants.prompt: A session ID must always reach the same server. Put the lookup in order.

items.text: Choose the session ID as the stable identity.
Apply the agreed hash function to get a ring position.
Walk clockwise to the first token at or after the position.
Route to that token’s physical node, then continue the replica walk if copies are stored.

variants.hint: Hashing comes before searching the sorted token map.
variants.explanation: Identity → hash position → successor token → physical node. The replica walk starts only after the first owner is found.

variants.title: Look up the owner
variants.context: Consistent hashing hashes keys and node tokens into one ordered space. A key belongs to the first token at or after its position, wrapping around at the end. Every participant must use the same hash and token map.
variants.prompt: A tenant ID selects a storage node. Put the lookup in order.

items.text: Start from the tenant ID that needs stable affinity.
Compute its hash position on the ring.
Binary-search the sorted token list for the successor token, wrapping if none is larger.
Deliver the request to the node that owns that token.

variants.hint: The sorted token list is searched with the hash position, not the raw ID.
variants.explanation: Key → position → successor search in the sorted token list → owner. A sorted list makes the lookup O(log T) for T tokens.

variants.title: Estimate the movement
variants.context: Adding one equally weighted node to N balanced nodes tends to move about 1/(N+1) of the keys to the new node. Plain hash(key) mod N moves most keys when N changes.
variants.prompt: A ring has 4 balanced nodes. You add a fifth with equal weight. About what percentage of keys move to the new node?
variants.hint: Adding one node to N balanced nodes moves about 1/(N+1) of the keys.
variants.explanation: 1/(4+1) = 20%. Only the ranges whose owner changed move; the other 80% stay put.

mistakes.feedback: About 80% is what hash(key) mod N would move when N goes from 4 to 5. The ring moves the complement.
1/N would be right for removing a node; adding one divides by N+1.
Answer in percent, not as a fraction.

variants.title: Estimate the movement
variants.context: Adding one equally weighted node to N balanced nodes tends to move about 1/(N+1) of the keys to the new node. Plain hash(key) mod N moves most keys when N changes.
variants.prompt: A ring has 9 balanced nodes. You add a tenth with equal weight. About what percentage of keys move to the new node?
variants.hint: Adding one node to N balanced nodes moves about 1/(N+1) of the keys.
variants.explanation: 1/(9+1) = 10%. The new node takes a slice from each neighbouring range it lands in; the rest of the ring is untouched.

mistakes.feedback: That is roughly what a modulo layout would move; the ring keeps 90% of keys where they were.
1/9 describes removing one of nine nodes; adding one divides by ten.
Answer in percent, not as a fraction.

variants.title: Estimate the movement
variants.context: Adding one equally weighted node to N balanced nodes tends to move about 1/(N+1) of the keys to the new node. Plain hash(key) mod N moves most keys when N changes.
variants.prompt: A ring has 3 balanced nodes. One node is removed. About what percentage of keys change owner?
variants.hint: Removing a balanced node moves that node’s prior share, about 1/N.
variants.explanation: The removed node owned about a third of the keys, so about 33% move to its successors. Nothing else changes owner.

mistakes.feedback: Two thirds of the keys still belong to the surviving nodes and stay put.
1/(N+1) is for adding a node; removal moves the node’s own share, 1/N.
Half would be far more than the node ever owned.

variants.title: Change membership safely
variants.context: Membership change is a control-plane operation: publish a versioned token map, stream the affected ranges, switch routing under an explicit handoff, then retire old copies after verification.
variants.prompt: Node D joins the ring. Order the control-plane steps.

items.text: Publish the new token map with a version so stale routers can be detected.
Stream the changing ranges while the old owner still serves them.
Switch authoritative routing under an explicit handoff contract.
Retire the old copies after integrity and replica counts are verified.

variants.hint: Nothing should move until every router can tell old and new maps apart.
variants.explanation: Version → transfer → cut over → verify. Deleting old copies before verification would turn a routine join into data loss.

variants.title: Change membership safely
variants.context: Membership change is a control-plane operation: publish a versioned token map, stream the affected ranges, switch routing under an explicit handoff, then retire old copies after verification.
variants.prompt: Node C is being retired. Order the control-plane steps.

items.text: Version and publish the token map without C.
Copy C’s ranges to their new owners with bounded bandwidth.
Move reads and writes to the new owners with a defined reconciliation rule for in-flight writes.
Delete C’s data only after routing and checksums are proven.

variants.hint: Transfer happens while the old owner can still answer requests.
variants.explanation: Publish → stream → cut over → retire. Bounding transfer bandwidth protects the live request budget during the move.

variants.title: Change membership safely
variants.context: Membership change is a control-plane operation: publish a versioned token map, stream the affected ranges, switch routing under an explicit handoff, then retire old copies after verification.
variants.prompt: A rebalance is adding virtual positions to an under-used node. Order the steps.

items.text: Publish the new token map with an epoch.
Stream the ranges that changed owner.
Cut routing over under the handoff contract.
Verify, then retire the previous ownership.

variants.hint: An epoch on the map comes first; retirement comes last.
variants.explanation: Same four steps, same order: version, transfer, cut over, verify and retire.

variants.title: Choose the placement family
variants.context: A ring gives elastic key affinity. Fixed hash slots give operators explicit resharding. Plain load balancing suits requests that need no key affinity. Virtual nodes balance ownership; they do not split a single hot key.
variants.prompt: Redis Cluster spreads keys over 16,384 hash slots that operators move explicitly. Which placement family is that?
options: Fixed hash slots with explicit resharding.
optionFeedback: Redis Cluster documents a fixed slot space and states that it does not use consistent hashing.
Redis Cluster is explicit that it does not use a consistent-hash ring.
Redis keys need affinity to a slot owner; stateless balancing would not work.
variants.hint: Who decides when a key range moves: a hash of the membership, or an operator?
variants.explanation: A fixed slot space keeps movement under operator control. Redis Cluster uses 16,384 slots and explicitly does not use consistent hashing.

variants.title: Choose the placement family
variants.context: A ring gives elastic key affinity. Fixed hash slots give operators explicit resharding. Plain load balancing suits requests that need no key affinity. Virtual nodes balance ownership; they do not split a single hot key.
variants.prompt: One key is far hotter than the rest and overloads its owner. Will adding virtual nodes fix it?
options: No. Virtual nodes balance aggregate ownership; they do not split one key across owners.
Yes. More tokens divide the key among nodes.
Yes, once the replication factor is raised.
optionFeedback: A single key always hashes to one position; virtual nodes change how ranges are shared, not where one key lands.
A key has exactly one hash position, so it still has one owner.
Replicas add copies for reads and durability; the write for that key still lands on one owner.
variants.hint: Where does one key hash to, no matter how many tokens exist?
variants.explanation: Virtual nodes improve distribution of many keys. A hot single key needs separate handling, such as splitting it in the application or caching it.

variants.title: Choose the placement family
variants.context: A ring gives elastic key affinity. Fixed hash slots give operators explicit resharding. Plain load balancing suits requests that need no key affinity. Virtual nodes balance ownership; they do not split a single hot key.
variants.prompt: Stateless API requests need no key affinity, and live load varies by the second. Which approach fits best?
options: Ordinary load balancing such as round robin or least request.
A consistent-hash ring with many virtual nodes.
A partition directory keyed by request ID.
optionFeedback: Without an affinity requirement, a balancer can react to live load directly.
A ring pins requests to owners; that only helps when something must stay on one node.
A directory adds critical metadata for a placement that nothing needs.
variants.hint: Does anything here need to land on the same node twice?
variants.explanation: A ring earns its metadata cost only when keys need stable affinity. Stateless requests are better served by a balancer that watches live load.

variants.title: Count real copies
variants.context: A ring can nominate several tokens for one key, but adjacent tokens may belong to the same physical node. Counting tokens instead of nodes creates false durability.
variants.prompt: Replication factor is 3. A naive walk stops after three tokens owned by nodes A, A, and B. How many distinct physical copies does the key really have?
variants.explanation: Two tokens belong to A, so only A and B hold the key: two real copies, not three. Production systems skip duplicate physical owners.

mistakes.feedback: Three tokens, but two of them sit on the same machine. A single failure of A leaves one copy.

variants.title: Count real copies
variants.context: A ring can nominate several tokens for one key, but adjacent tokens may belong to the same physical node. Counting tokens instead of nodes creates false durability.
variants.prompt: Replication factor is 3. Walking clockwise, the tokens belong to nodes B, B, B, C, A. A correct walk skips duplicate nodes. How many tokens does it visit before it holds three distinct copies?
variants.hint: Keep walking until three different nodes have been selected.
variants.explanation: B is selected once and skipped twice, then C, then A. That takes five token visits for three distinct copies.

mistakes.feedback: Three visits would give B, B, B: one physical copy.
After four visits only B and C are selected; A is the fifth token.

variants.title: Count real copies
variants.context: A ring can nominate several tokens for one key, but adjacent tokens may belong to the same physical node. Counting tokens instead of nodes creates false durability.
variants.prompt: Replication factor is 2. Both nodes selected by a correct walk sit in the same rack, and the rack loses power. How many copies remain reachable?
variants.hint: Distinct nodes are necessary but not sufficient; the failure boundary matters too.
variants.explanation: Distinct nodes in one rack share a failure domain, so both copies vanish together. Topology-aware placement spreads copies across racks or datacenters.

mistakes.feedback: Both nodes are in the failed rack, so neither copy is reachable.
Nothing survives a failure domain that contains every copy.
